draft.body:
On October 12, 2026, Microsoft officially announced the Azure Maia 300, its third-generation custom artificial intelligence accelerator engineered to handle long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational interfaces, and sustained agentic workloads. Microsoft revealed comprehensive rack-level specifications, memory configurations, and deployment schedules. The company plans to begin production rollouts in 2027, scaling the platform into multi-gigawatt installations that could potentially involve more than one million chips serving internal AI operations across Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Azure OpenAI workloads, and proprietary MAI models.

According to [The Official Microsoft Blog](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2026/10/12/microsoft-to-expand-azure-maia-system-to-multi-gigawatt-deployments/), Maia 300 is designed to serve as Microsoft's primary inference architecture as enterprise demands shift toward multi-step autonomous agents. The announcement follows the production deployment of Maia 200, which currently serves live workloads for Microsoft Copilot, Teams, and internal foundation model research across data centers in the United States, Europe, and Australia.

[[FIG1]]

## Multi-Chiplet Architecture Built on TSMC 2nm

To manage manufacturing economics while scaling compute capability, Microsoft adopted a disaggregated multi-chiplet architecture for Maia 300. As detailed in the [Microsoft Azure Blog](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/blog/deep-dive-into-azure-maia-300-architecture/), the primary compute chiplets are fabricated on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's (TSMC) advanced N2P process node. Peripheral functions, including memory controllers and input/output (I/O) communication blocks, reside on separate dies manufactured on 3-nanometer technology.

This separation allows Microsoft to dedicate silicon area on the costliest cutting-edge node exclusively to compute execution. The design increases raw compute FLOPs by 36 percent over the previous-generation Maia 200 while expanding scale-up interconnect bandwidth by 14 percent, according to Microsoft's architectural whitepaper. Control path programming remains separated from data path execution through Microsoft's Software Defined Locally Accessed (SDLA) architecture, which coordinates data placement and DMA engines across specialized local memories and compute engines, while superpod communication between accelerators occurs without host processor involvement.

On-package memory organization also shifts away from uniform memory access (UMA). Instead, Maia 300 adopts a locality-aware non-uniform memory access (NUMA) topology across the chiplet substrate. Each compute region pairs with adjacent memory storage to limit physical travel distance across the package, minimizing electrical dissipation during decode-heavy token generation.

## HBM4 Subsystems and Low-Precision Compute

Memory bandwidth forms the central constraint in cloud-scale large language model serving. Maia 300 integrates eight stacks of next-generation HBM4 memory, delivering 288 GB of high-bandwidth memory capacity and 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth. As reported by [TrendForce](https://www.trendforce.com/news/2026/10/13/news-ai-chip-memory-strategies-diverge-microsofts-maia-300-fuels-hbm4-demand-as-intel-bets-on-lower-cost-lpddr5x/), this represents an expansion from the six HBM3E stacks deployed on Maia 200, which provided 216 GB of memory.

The accelerator operates within a thermal design power (TDP) envelope of 950 watts per chip. Compared to Maia 200, Microsoft states the new subsystem provides 2.5 times the total memory bandwidth, a 33 percent capacity increase, and approximately double the HBM bandwidth per watt. The hardware architecture pairs this capacity with software-managed on-die static random-access memory (SRAM), which functions as a dedicated scratchpad to shelter HBM from continuous access during intermediate kernel operations.

[[FIG2]]

To increase sequence length capabilities, Maia 300 adds instruction set architecture (ISA) extensions tailored for low-precision mathematical formats. The chip natively accelerates enhanced Microscaling FP4 (MXFP4) computation and sub-3-bit storage formats for key-value (KV) caches. Designing for low-precision formats reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for computation and KV-cache storage.

## Rack Density and 12,288-Chip Superpod Fabrics

At the data center level, Microsoft packages the accelerators into integrated rack systems designed around power and cooling constraints. Each Maia 300 rack houses 96 accelerators divided among 24 four-accelerator trays, drawing 167 kilowatts of power. This doubles the accelerator density of the Maia 200 platform. Each tray includes its own host processor, storage, memory, and thermal routing, removing the requirement for standalone host compute shelves.

Across a single 96-accelerator rack, the system delivers an aggregate 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth. Power enters through dual utility feeds supported by a 50-volt busbar distribution system and an integrated rack-level automatic transfer switch. Thermal dissipation uses a hybrid model: facility liquid cooling dissipates more than 80 percent of the heat load generated by compute processors, voltage regulators, and networking ASICs, while supplemental air cooling manages peripheral storage and auxiliary chips.

Interconnect scaling uses a two-tier Ethernet-based AI transport fabric. Accelerators communicate directly within trays over short electrical links, while three liquid-cooled switch trays containing six high-radix ASICs connect all 96 chips inside a single rack pod. To scale beyond individual cabinets, optical transceivers link up to 128 racks together, creating a unified scale-up domain of 12,288 accelerators. According to Microsoft's technical disclosure, an accelerator can route up to 750 GB/s to any peer within this superpod fabric without traversing standard host-level network interface cards.

## Efficiency Claims and Market Context

Microsoft claims that Maia 300 delivers up to seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200 and more than 2.5 times the performance per watt. Against external competitors, Microsoft projects that Maia 300 will achieve 40 percent more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. However, as noted in reporting by [Reuters](https://cio.economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/next-gen-technologies/microsoft-plans-huge-deployment-of-its-own-ai-chips-with-an-eye-on-saving-costs/134906279), Microsoft did not disclose the specific competitive GPU configurations or cluster baselines used to calculate that figure.

Rani Borkar, president of Azure hardware systems and infrastructure at Microsoft, explained the design focus to Reuters, stating: "It's basically delivering more intelligence for every watt, every dollar, and every byte of memory by optimizing across the entire system."

Market observers note that physical density carries tradeoffs. As covered by [Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/microsofts-maia-300-chip-and-what-it-means-for-nvidia-93CH-4944991), a 96-chip Maia 300 rack consumes approximately 167 kW, compared to roughly 142 kW drawn by Nvidia's 72-GPU GB300 server rack. Financial analysts also highlighted that while hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta continue developing internal silicon to mitigate capital costs—Microsoft expects annual capital expenditures to exceed $175 billion—Nvidia maintains a lead in AI training, while customer adoption will be key for Maia. On the day of the announcement, Microsoft shares rose 0.86 percent to trade at $539.66, while Nvidia shares traded down 1.22 percent at $226.49.

## Deployment Timelines and Workload Allocation

Microsoft stated that Maia 300 production deployments will begin in 2027. Ahead of that rollout, Microsoft is expanding its Maia 200 footprint. Production workloads currently active on Maia 200 include Microsoft Copilot, Teams AI features, and inference and data generation for the MAI research group. Workloads for GitHub Copilot and the Microsoft Foundry model platform are scheduled to transition onto Maia 200 infrastructure before the end of 2026, while Dragon Copilot is designed to be supported across the Maia generations.

When Maia 300 enters production facilities in 2027, Microsoft plans to allocate both internal services and partner models—including proprietary models from OpenAI—onto the multi-gigawatt footprint. Microsoft will share information on its AI strategy, technology adoption trends, and success in Frontier Transformation at Microsoft Ignite 2026 in San Francisco.
